events.title: Alasdair's small hulls
events.body: On the strand below Seann Skell the boat-wright Alasdair mac Iain builds hulls no longer than his arm on spines of oak and floats them in the river pool and the river mouth, to learn what a keel does. He finds that a keel makes a hull stiff and lets it be built bigger.

events.title: Mòrag undertakes to pay for the oaks
events.body: At Inis àrsaidh Mòrag nic Dhòmhnaill and Aonghas mac Fhionnlaigh hear Alasdair out and send him to look at the grove of Doire fhionn. Mòrag undertakes to pay for the felling and hauling out of her own silver.

events.title: The naming of the trees
events.body: Eilidh nic Ruairidh, keeper of the grove of Doire fhionn, makes Alasdair choose each oak he will take and hear its name. He chooses fifty-four and leaves one young tree, the Child, standing alone.

events.title: The felling of the Queen
events.body: Eighty men of the households of the roll fell the grove of Doire fhionn through the summer, each tree onto a bed of brush. The greatest, called the Queen, takes two days to bring down.

events.title: The ox-sleds on the north road
events.body: The keel-timbers are dragged forty-two miles south to the sea on sleds of oak shod with ash, six yoke to a sled. The road is widened at every bend and a causeway built over the stream below Doire fhionn.

events.title: Woodcutters' huts at Doire fhiadhaich
events.body: Woodcutters of the roll build huts at the edge of a wild oak wood on the shore of Loch chrom to fell crooked oak for the fleet's frames and knees. They go home when the felling is done and the huts fall in; the wood keeps its name.

events.title: The bed of the first keel
events.body: Alasdair levels a line of oak blocks on the strand above the high-water mark and digs a saw-pit beside it. The Queen oak is rolled onto the blocks and hewn to a keel with a ridge along its underside.

events.title: Coinneach mac Fhearghais sworn
events.body: At the feast of Lugh the wrights of the strand bind themselves into one fellowship. A custodian of Taigh na Fèithe swears their apprentices over a coal, and the first sworn is Coinneach mac Fhearghais, a coaster-wright's son of fourteen.

events.title: The first frames stand on the strand
events.body: By the moon of Pailteach the first frames rise from the keel in pairs, pegged with heart-oak. The harbour scribe writes that the hull looks like the ribs of a great beast picked clean on the shore.

events.title: The Child walled
events.body: The village of Doire fhionn builds a low wall of stones round the one young oak left on the grove hill, and its old keeper sits beside it every evening until dark.

events.title: Alasdair walks north with a knotted line
events.body: In the moon of Gearras, after Là Fhèill Brìde, Alasdair mac Iain sets out alone on the north road with a pack, a staff and a line knotted every arm's length for measuring, making fifteen miles the first day and sleeping in a byre.

events.title: An Fhaoileag launched
events.body: The first deep-keeled hull, planked and rigged, is floated off the blocks below Seann Skell with a coal from Taigh na Fèithe set at her step. The town calls her An Fhaoileag, the gull, for the way she rides the water.

events.title: The nine named at Inis àrsaidh
events.body: The roll-keeper of Inis àrsaidh cuts eleven names into the village's board on the night of the drowning, the village sitting up with her as the custom asks. Alasdair's sister's son Tormod Beag is among the eight bodies brought back; three more are never found.

events.title: The keening at Inis àrsaidh
events.body: The eight recovered dead are keened on the shingle under sailcloth and a lamp at each head; for the three never found a single lamp is lit and burns down unwatched. Alasdair stays three days doing whatever the village asks of him.

events.title: Households struck and households entered
events.body: Eleven households strike themselves from the Seann Skell roll after word of the drowning, and eleven others enter in the same weeks, among them kin of a survivor and a widow of Ros bheag who gives her daughters' names. Calum mac Nèill records both counts without comment.

events.title: The second keel laid to the changed pattern
events.body: Alasdair Saor lays a second keel on the strand below Seann Skell, built to the fuller, hollow-bowed run he redrew by a driftwood fire after the drowning. Mòrag nic Dhòmhnaill sends silver again to see her built.

events.title: The rope-walks learn the names of a keel
events.body: After shroud-lines sent west from Cuan shean fail within a season, the wrights walk the rope-walks and name the parts of a hull to the spinners and walkers. Iain Ròpaire, master of the walks, takes to walking one himself to learn the words in his own hands.

events.title: Birth of Raghnall mac Uilleim
events.body: A son, Raghnall, is born at Cathair dhearg to Queen Beathag nic Dhòmhnaill and her consort Uilleam mac Iain, in the queen's sixteenth year crowned and her own thirtieth year of life.

events.title: The sail-cloth tallies at Baile àrsaidh
events.body: The shire seat's tally-keeper cuts notches for close-woven lengths from households across Siorrachd Baile àrsaidh, far more than expected, some sent by weavers with no kin on the roll and no thought of sailing. The sticks fill a chest that wants a second lid.

events.title: An Dara Fhaoileag planked
events.body: An Dara Fhaoileag stands planked from keel to sheer and steps her mast on the strand below Seann Skell. The wrights name her An Dara Fhaoileag, the second gull, and the doubt among the older wrights over her fuller, hollow-bowed lines goes quiet.

events.title: Six pilots sent east to Cuan ruadh
events.body: Fearchar mac Ruairidh finds that no pilot of the west coast has ever held a course by night, and six are chosen to walk the hundred miles to the old steersmen of Cuan ruadh: two of Ceann mhòr, two of Ros bheag, one of Cuan shean, and Catrìona nic Iain, who asks to be sent before she is asked.

events.title: The six pilots reach Cuan ruadh
events.body: After seven days on foot over the mountain country the six pilots come down to Cuan ruadh on the eastern coast and are given lodging without question. They are sent, the next morning, to the steersman Seumas Reultach.

events.title: Seumas Reultach begins the teaching
events.body: On the headland above Cuan ruadh the old steersman Seumas Reultach begins teaching the six pilots the wheel of the sky and Reul na Stiùire, by which it is held. Most of what he gives them is spoken, night after night, and set down nowhere.

events.title: Part of the star-lore set on hide
events.body: At Taigh na Fèithe's asking, Seumas Reultach has his granddaughter cut onto a scraped hide the wheel of the sky, Reul na Stiùire and the four turning marks of the year. He keeps back the swell-reading and the wind-smell, saying some things a hide can hold and some things only a life can.

events.title: Death of Seumas Reultach
events.body: In the moon of Faolach the old steersman of Cuan ruadh dies on the cliff path above the town where he taught the six pilots the stars, and is buried there among his own people. His granddaughter gives the hide of star-marks into Catrìona nic Iain's keeping to carry west.

events.title: The pilots return west
events.body: The six pilots cross the mountain country again to the west coast, carrying the hide of star-marks and what they have learned of the wheel of the sky, Reul na Stiùire and the smell of the dark before a change of wind.

events.title: The first night-steering trial off Ros àrsaidh
events.body: Off Ros àrsaidh two boats go out after dark, one steered close along the shore by lantern, the other by Catrìona nic Iain alone by Reul na Stiùire with every lantern doused. She brings her boat home first, exactly where and when she had said she would.

events.title: Catrìona nic Iain made pilot of An Ròn Glas
events.body: Catrìona nic Iain reaches Seann Skell after the households of the roll have chosen Mòrag nic Dhòmhnaill and Fearchar mac Ruairidh to lead them. On the west quay Mòrag asks her to be pilot of her hull, An Ròn Glas, and Catrìona names her Reul na Stiùire.
